event: The Ottoman conquest finds the Samaritans a scattered remnant of ~500, spread across Nablus, Gaza, Damascus, and Cairo.
High Priest Pinḥas is exiled to Damascus — leadership disruption under early Ottoman rule.

event: For tax purposes the Ottoman authorities classed the Samaritans as part of the Jews — the status-by-association that would later let Chief Rabbi Gagin rescue them in 1842. Many Samaritans served as government finance officials, especially in Damascus, and firmans addressed complaints about their treatment of taxpayers (e.g. the order of 10 October 1565 to the governor and qadi of Damascus). A reminder the community was not only preyed upon but, in places, fiscally empowered.

passages.text: For tax purposes the Samaritans were seen by the Ottoman authorities as part of the Jews. Many were employed as government officials in charge of finances, especially in Damascus. Numerous complaints about their treatment of the taxpayers were addressed in firmans. event: Under the Tuqan and Jarrar governors, Muslims plunder the High Priest's house and the ritual bath and seize houses, vineyards, fields and 'countless goods' — and forcibly convert many Samaritans.
quote: Ils convertirent par force beaucoup de Samaritains. (They forcibly converted many Samaritans.)

event: Sultan Mehmed IV forbids access to Mount Gerizim, forcing the Passover sacrifice onto the mountain's eastern slope — a dated central-authority religious ban.

event: The Damascus community disappears, substantially by conversion to Islam: several prominent Muslim families of Damascus (Dar Gofari, Dar Nahas, Dar Rumah, Dar Mneid) are of Samaritan origin — the apostasy ratchet visible in family genealogies.

event: A Jerusalem-mufti fatwa affirms the Samaritans as People of the Book — an intermittent legal floor; they are taxed alongside the Jews.

event: The Cairo Samaritan synagogue is handed over to the local Jewish community — no Samaritans left in Cairo.
During Napoleon's invasion local Arabs seize the property of the Gaza community; by now the diaspora has contracted to Nablus alone — 'the only place in the entire world' where Samaritans remain.
The wealthy Shelaby / Danfī bankers — the community's de-facto leaders and bankers to the Nablus governors — are repeatedly extorted, arrested, and (1805, 1813) murdered.
Persecution under the governors 'Abdul Hady and Moosa Bek' — named by Mills as an earlier crisis a generation before the 1841 extirpation plot.

event: The Egyptian decade under Ibrahim Pasha is the one window of relief — in the community's own chronicle, his just and equitable government relieved the Samaritans 'of the tyranny of the peoples inhabiting this country.' An inverted pasha-cascade: here the Egyptian rule itself was the opening, and its end the catastrophe.
quote: …the Samaritans were relieved of the tyranny of the peoples inhabiting this country, for his government was just and equitable.

event: On the Egyptian withdrawal, the Muslim inhabitants of Nablus vent their hatred of the toppled Egyptians in a pogrom against the Samaritans — whose notables had been the visible non-Muslim functionaries of the regime.

event: The extirpation crisis: the ʿulamāʾ rule the Samaritans 'had no religion at all' — not People of the Book but pagans 'whom every true believer was commanded to convert or exterminate.' A widow's son Isaac is imprisoned, lashed, and forcibly converted (renamed 'Asaad'); her daughter dies of fear of the torture.

event: Rescue: the Sephardi Chief Rabbi of Jerusalem, Haim Avraham Gagin, issues a written declaration that 'the Samaritan people is a branch of the children of Israel' — refuting the ʿulamāʾ and giving the community just enough theological cover to survive. (The ruling is still cited in Israeli religious-status debates.)

event: British consular protection: Consul James Finn intervenes; the agent Jacob esh-Shellaby carries a petition to London; Lord Clarendon sends £50 with orders to use 'good offices to save the Samaritan people from persecution, from whatever quarter,' and Stratford de Redcliffe presses the Porte.

John Mills, living among the community, counts 40 families / ~150 souls in a 'ghetto-like' quarter at the foot of Gerizim (+1 by 1860).

event: The Ottoman state pacifies the Nablus district by force, breaks the local feudal lords, and installs direct rule — beginning an unaccustomed 'deep peace' that runs to WWI.
The community reaches its all-time low — about 85 souls — with a male-to-female ratio approaching 2:1; extinction is widely forecast and never arrives.

passages.text: The number of the Samaritans by that time had dwindled to 195 individuals or fewer.144 Extinction seemed inevitable to many onlookers. To quote only one such prediction, by John Mills in his book Three Months’ Residence at Nablus: “before many generations more have passed away, this nation, in all probability, will have become extinct.”145 Although Mills lived with them in 1855 and 1860, many years later scholars and others made similar forecasts. event: Historic nadir, ~140 souls; the American philanthropist E. K. Warren, 'amazed and enchanted' to find them surviving into the 20th century, builds medical and educational facilities, aiding recovery.

passages.text: Jews and Christians, were a people of the Book and ought not be persecuted; and the American E. K. Warren built medical and educational facilities for the fragile community at the beginning of the twentieth century.

event: Abraham b. Marḥiv Tsedaka settles in Jaffa (attempts 1894, 1902; success 1905) — the nucleus of the modern second Samaritan centre (later Tel Aviv, then Ḥolon 1951).

The old Nablus synagogue is damaged in the magnitude-6.2 July earthquake — relief in this window came less from any change of heart among neighbours than from restored central order plus outside patronage.

passages.text: Nablus had a very old synagogue, located in the west of the city in the Samaritan neighborhood, next to the Yasminah neighborhood, which was damaged in the strong earthquake (magnitude 6.2) of July 1927.102 However, the Samaritans continued to worship in it, and only in 1947 was it partially repaired.
